stimuli.title: Bees on the farm
stimuli.content:
Most farmers think of bees, if they think of them at all, as insects that sting. Yet a large share of the fruits, vegetables and oilseeds grown in India depends on bees and other insects to carry pollen from one flower to another. Without this service, which nature provides free of charge, many plants would produce fewer and smaller fruits, or none at all.

In recent years, beekeepers and scientists have noticed that wild bees are becoming harder to find in many farming areas. The reasons are not fully understood, but the loss of hedges and wild plants at the edges of fields, and the careless spraying of pesticides at times when bees are active, are thought to play a large part. A field that is sprayed in the middle of a sunny morning may lose its visiting bees in a single day.

Some farmers have responded by keeping bees themselves. A few wooden boxes placed at the edge of a mustard or sunflower field can raise the yield of the crop, and the honey and wax they produce can be sold for extra income. Training in beekeeping is offered by agricultural universities and voluntary groups, and the cost of starting is modest compared with most other farm businesses. Women in several villages have formed groups that manage the boxes together and share the earnings.

Beekeeping is not without difficulties. The bees must be moved or fed when flowers are scarce, the boxes must be checked regularly for disease, and the honey market is crowded with cheap, adulterated products that pull down the price for genuine producers. A beekeeper who cannot prove the purity of her honey may find it hard to earn a fair price.

Still, the lesson of the bee box is a useful one. A farm is not a factory that runs on seeds, water and fertiliser alone. It depends on living helpers that ask for little except flowers and a little care, and a farmer who looks after them is also looking after the harvest.

stimuli.title: Grandparents go online
stimuli.content:
When Kamala Devi, a retired schoolteacher of sixty-eight, received a smartphone from her son, she kept it in its box for three months. She was afraid of pressing the wrong button and losing money, and she did not want to keep asking her busy grandchildren for help. Her story is common. Millions of older Indians now own smartphones, but many use them only to receive calls.

This matters more than it might seem. Pensions are credited to bank accounts, electricity bills and medical appointments are increasingly handled through apps, and family news is shared in video calls and messages. An older person who cannot use these services must depend on others for tasks that she once managed alone. For many, the loss of independence is harder to bear than the inconvenience.

Some cities and towns now run free classes for senior citizens, often held in community halls and parks. Volunteers, many of them college students, sit with small groups and go through one task at a time: making a video call, reading a message, booking a doctor's appointment. Learners are also shown how to enlarge the text on the screen and how to type by speaking, which helps those with weak eyesight or unsteady hands. The classes move slowly, and nobody is laughed at for asking the same question twice.

Kamala Devi joined such a class last year. Within a few weeks she was sending voice messages to her sister in another state, and she now pays her own electricity bill from her phone. What helped her most, she says, was not the technology itself but the patience of the young volunteer who taught her. 'At home, everyone was in a hurry,' she explains. 'Here, I was allowed to be slow.'

The volunteers say they learn as much as they teach. Many had never spent long hours with anyone of their grandparents' age, and they discover stories, advice and humour they had not expected. A class meant to close a digital gap, it turns out, can close other gaps too.

stimuli.title: The cost of noise
stimuli.content:
Ask residents of an Indian city what troubles them most, and they will probably mention traffic, dust or the price of housing. Noise is rarely near the top of the list. People have come to accept the blare of horns, the roar of generators and the loudspeakers of weddings and festivals as part of urban life, as unavoidable as the weather. Yet a growing body of research suggests that this acceptance comes at a price.

Noise does more than irritate. Long exposure to loud traffic at night disturbs sleep even when the sleeper does not fully wake, and poor sleep over months and years has been linked to high blood pressure and heart disease. Studies of schoolchildren in noisy neighbourhoods have found that they tend to score lower on reading tests than children in quieter areas, possibly because constant noise makes it harder to concentrate and to hear the teacher clearly. Workers exposed to loud machinery without protection may slowly lose part of their hearing without noticing until the damage is done.

India has had rules on noise for more than two decades. They set limits for different zones, with the strictest applying to areas around hospitals, schools and courts, and they restrict the use of loudspeakers late at night. The difficulty lies in enforcement. Measuring noise requires equipment and trained staff, offenders are many and scattered, and a police officer who stops a wedding procession for being too loud can expect little thanks from anyone.

Some cities have tried a different approach. Instead of relying only on fines, they have run campaigns against needless honking, installed displays at busy junctions showing the noise level as it happens, and declared 'silent zones' where horns are banned. In one experiment, signals at a junction were set to stay red longer whenever drivers honked continuously, so that honking only prolonged their own wait.

None of these measures will make a city quiet. But they treat noise as what it is: a form of pollution with real effects on health and learning, not merely a nuisance to be shrugged off. The first step towards a quieter city may simply be to stop regarding noise as normal.

stimuli.title: Water that never arrives
stimuli.content:
A city's water supply is usually judged by how much water it can draw from rivers, lakes and wells. Far less attention goes to what happens to that water after it leaves the treatment plant. In many Indian cities, a large share of the water that is pumped and treated never reaches a paying customer. Engineers call this 'non-revenue water', and in some cities it is estimated to be close to half of the total supply.

Part of the loss is physical. Old pipes crack, joints loosen and valves fail, and because most of the network lies underground, a leak can run for months before anyone notices. Part of it is commercial: water that does reach homes but is never billed, because meters are missing or broken, connections are illegal or records are out of date. Either way, the city pays to pump and clean water for which it earns nothing.

The consequences are felt by everyone. Because so much water is lost, supply is often rationed to a few hours a day. When the pipes are empty, the pressure inside them falls, and dirty water from the surrounding soil can be drawn in through the same cracks through which clean water escapes. Families respond by installing storage tanks and private pumps, which pull water unevenly and leave households at the end of the line with even less.

Reducing these losses is less glamorous than building a new dam or laying a pipeline from a distant river, and it rarely features in election speeches. It involves dividing the network into small zones, measuring how much water enters each, finding and repairing leaks block by block, and fixing meters and billing records. The work is slow and its results are invisible to the public. Yet every litre saved in this way is a litre that need not be found elsewhere, and it is usually far cheaper than a litre drawn from a new source.

A city that cannot account for its water may not need more of it as urgently as it thinks. It may first need to stop losing what it already has.

stimuli.title: The right to fail
stimuli.content:
Every economy that wants enterprise must decide what to do with those who try and fail. For much of history, the answer was harsh. Debtors who could not pay were imprisoned, their property seized and their names published as a warning to others. The assumption behind such treatment was that failure was a moral lapse, and that the prospect of disgrace would make borrowers more careful.

Modern insolvency law rests on a different premise. Most businesses fail not because their owners are dishonest but because markets change, customers disappear or a promising idea turns out to be ahead of, or behind, its time. If the penalty for such failure is ruin for life, the rational response is not greater care but greater timidity. Talented people will avoid starting firms, and those who do start them will cling to a sinking venture for too long, hoping to avoid the stigma of closure, while its assets lose value and its debts mount.

A well-designed system therefore tries to achieve two things at once. It must allow a failing firm to be resolved quickly, so that whatever value remains, in machines, buildings, a brand or a skilled workforce, can be sold or put to better use before it decays. And it must allow an honest entrepreneur, once the process is over, to start again without carrying the old debts for the rest of her life. The first goal protects creditors; the second protects the willingness to take risks on which economic growth depends.

The two goals are not always in harmony. Creditors who expect to recover little may be reluctant to lend at all, or may lend only at higher rates and against heavy collateral, which hurts precisely the small firms the system is meant to encourage. A discharge granted too easily, on the other hand, invites abuse by borrowers who take money with no intention of repaying it. The skill lies in separating misfortune from fraud, and that requires courts and tribunals with the time and expertise to examine each case on its merits.

Where the balance is struck well, failure becomes what it ought to be in a dynamic economy: an expensive lesson rather than a life sentence.

stimuli.title: Justice in one's own language
stimuli.content:
A villager who goes to court in India may find that the most important document in his case, the judgment, is written in a language he cannot read. In the higher courts, proceedings and judgments are largely in English, a language that only a small fraction of the population speaks with ease. Litigants must rely on lawyers to explain what has been decided about their own land, liberty or livelihood, and something is often lost, or added, in the explanation.

The argument for change rests on a simple principle: law that binds people should be intelligible to them. A citizen who cannot understand why a court ruled against him is less likely to accept the ruling as fair, and less able to judge whether an appeal is worthwhile. Justice, in this view, must not only be done and be seen to be done; it must also be understood.

Recent efforts to translate judgments into Indian languages, often with the help of software, are a step in this direction. Yet the translation of legal texts is unusually demanding. Legal terms carry precise meanings built up over decades of precedent, and a translation that is fluent but slightly inexact can mislead more dangerously than an awkward literal one. A word that suggests 'may' where the original says 'shall' can change a party's obligations entirely. For this reason, such translations are generally offered as an aid to understanding, while the English original remains the authoritative version.

Critics point out that this arrangement, however sensible, preserves the very hierarchy it is meant to soften: the version that counts is still the one most citizens cannot read. Supporters reply that perfection should not be the enemy of progress. A careful translation, checked by people who know both the law and the language, may not carry legal authority, but it gives the litigant something he did not have before: the ability to read, in his own words, the reasons for a decision that shapes his life.

stimuli.title: Learning to float
stimuli.content:
In many parts of rural India, children grow up close to water: village ponds, rivers, canals and, during the monsoon, flooded fields. Yet very few of them are ever taught to swim. Drowning is among the leading causes of death of young children in many countries, and India is no (1) ______. Most of these deaths happen quietly, close to home, often when an adult has looked away for only a few minutes.

Some voluntary groups have begun to teach swimming in a simple, low-cost way. Classes are held in shallow, fenced-off parts of ponds, and trainers use empty plastic bottles and old tyre tubes to help children (2) ______ while they learn. Children are first taught to stay calm in the water and to lie on their backs, since panic is often more dangerous than the water itself. Only then do they learn to move towards the bank.

Parents were (3) ______ at first. Many believed that a child who could swim would be tempted to go into deep water alone. Trainers answered this fear by teaching water safety along with swimming: never to swim without an adult nearby, to stay away from fast-flowing rivers, and to throw a rope or a bottle rather than jump in to (4) ______ a friend who is in trouble.

Another simple measure is supervision. In some villages, mothers take turns to look after young children in a crèche during the busiest working hours, so that toddlers are not left (5) ______ near water while adults are in the fields. Together, these steps cost very little, yet they can save lives that are too often lost for lack of a few hours of training and a watchful eye.

stimuli.title: Reading the label
stimuli.content:
Walk down the aisle of any supermarket and you will find packets covered in cheerful promises: 'natural', 'light', 'rich in fibre', 'no added sugar'. Such words are designed to catch the eye, but they reveal little about what is actually inside. The information that matters is usually printed in small type on the back of the pack, and few shoppers take the trouble to read it.

A food label, read carefully, can be surprisingly (1) ______. The list of ingredients is arranged in order of weight, so if sugar or oil appears near the top, the product contains more of it than of anything listed below. The nutrition table shows the amount of energy, fat, sugar and salt in every hundred grams, which allows two products to be (2) ______ fairly even when their packs are of different sizes. A biscuit sold as a healthy choice may, on inspection, contain as much sugar as an ordinary cream biscuit.

Manufacturers, however, have learned to (3) ______ these rules. Sugar may be split into several forms, such as glucose, invert syrup and malt extract, so that none of them appears high in the list on its own. Serving sizes may be set unrealistically small, making the figures per serving look modest. A drink labelled 'no added sugar' may still be heavily sweetened with fruit concentrate.

For these reasons, many nutrition experts favour simple warnings on the front of the pack, such as a symbol showing that a product is high in salt or sugar. Such labels can be understood at a glance, even by a shopper in a hurry or one who does not read well. The industry has generally (4) ______ them, arguing that they unfairly brand foods as unhealthy. Evidence from countries that have adopted them suggests that they do change what people buy, and that manufacturers often respond by quietly (5) ______ their recipes to contain less salt and sugar, a change that benefits even those customers who never read the label.

stimuli.title: The case for the index fund
stimuli.content:
An investor who buys shares through a mutual fund usually pays a professional manager to pick the companies most likely to do well. It seems a **(1) sensible** arrangement: experts with research teams should be able to beat ordinary savers. Yet study after study, in many countries, has found that most actively managed funds fail to outperform the market index they are measured against, especially over long periods and once their fees are **(2) ignored**.

The reason is partly arithmetic. The market as a whole is made up of all investors together, so before costs the average actively managed rupee must earn roughly the market return. After fees, which can amount to a couple of per cent a year, the average active investor must therefore do **(3) better** than the market. A few managers will beat it in any given year, but picking them in advance has proved remarkably difficult, and past winners often become future laggards.

An index fund takes the opposite approach. Instead of trying to pick winners, it simply buys all the shares in an index, such as the fifty largest companies on an exchange, in the same proportions. Because it needs no research team and trades rarely, its costs are a **(4) fraction** of those of an active fund. Over twenty or thirty years, that difference, compounded, can add up to a substantial sum.

Index funds are not without **(5) merits**. An investor who owns the whole market owns its weaker companies along with its stronger ones, and has no protection when the market as a whole falls. Some critics also argue that if everyone invested passively, nobody would be left to study companies and set prices sensibly. For the ordinary saver, however, such concerns are remote. The more immediate danger is paying high fees for skill that may not exist, and the humble index fund offers a cheap and **(6) opaque** way to avoid it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what service do bees provide to crops?

options.text: They feed on the pests that attack fruit and vegetable crops.
They improve the quality of the soil in which the plants grow.
They carry pollen between flowers, which helps the plants produce fruit.
They shade young plants from the strong heat of the sun.

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 says crops depend on bees 'to carry pollen from one flower to another', and that without this service many plants would produce fewer and smaller fruits, or none at all.
steps: Without it, fewer fruits: option C
solution.why_others_wrong: Eating pests (A), improving soil (B) and shading plants (D) are never mentioned as things bees do.
solution.final_answer: Option C: They carry pollen between flowers, which helps the plants produce fruit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following does the passage mention as a likely reason why wild bees are becoming harder to find?

options.text: Spraying pesticides at times when bees are active
Farmers harvesting too much honey from wild hives
Unusually cold winters in farming areas
Too many bee boxes placed at the edges of fields

solution.concept: Locating a stated cause
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 names two likely reasons: the loss of hedges and wild plants at field edges, and 'the careless spraying of pesticides at times when bees are active'.
steps: Find 'wild bees are becoming harder to find' in paragraph 2
Reasons given: loss of hedges; careless spraying
Option A matches the second reason
solution.why_others_wrong: B and C are not mentioned. D reverses the passage: bee boxes are a response by farmers, not a cause of the decline.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Spraying pesticides at times when bees are active

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, may a beekeeper find it hard to earn a fair price for her honey?

options.text: Universities buy most of the honey from beekeepers at a fixed, very low price.
Most people in India prefer sugar to honey and buy very little of it.
Honey spoils quickly in hot weather and cannot be stored for long.
Fake honey drags prices down, and she may be unable to show that hers is pure.

solution.concept: Inference: linking two sentences in the same paragraph
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says cheap, adulterated products 'pull down the price for genuine producers', and a beekeeper 'who cannot prove the purity of her honey may find it hard to earn a fair price'.
steps: Problem 1: cheap, adulterated honey lowers prices
Problem 2: genuine producers must prove purity
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are not stated anywhere. Universities offer training, not a market for honey.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Fake honey drags prices down, and she may be unable to show that hers is pure.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'modest' as used in the passage ('the cost of starting is modest compared with most other farm businesses')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: modest (of an amount) = not large
solution.explanation: The sentence compares the cost of starting beekeeping with that of other farm businesses and presents it as an advantage. Here 'modest' describes an amount, so it means small or moderate.
steps: 'modest' here describes a cost, not a person
Presented as an advantage → the cost is low
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Shy' is a meaning of 'modest' only when it describes a person. 'Enormous' is the opposite. 'Boastful' is the opposite of the personal sense of 'modest'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: How to Make Honey at Home

solution.concept: A title must cover the main idea of the whole passage
solution.explanation: The passage explains how much crops depend on bees, why wild bees are declining, how keeping bees helps farmers and what difficulties it brings, ending with the idea that bees are 'living helpers that ask for little'.
steps: Para 1: bees pollinate crops for free
Paras 2–4: decline of wild bees; beekeeping and its problems
Para 5: bees as helpers of the farm: option A
solution.why_others_wrong: B is not discussed. C picks up only the opening remark about stings. D goes beyond the passage, which criticises careless spraying but never calls for a ban.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Bees: The Farmer's Unpaid Helpers

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why did Kamala Devi keep her new smartphone in its box for three months?

options.text: The phone did not work properly in her area, where the signal was weak.
She feared losing money by a wrong press and did not want to trouble her grandchildren.
Her son had asked her not to use it until he could show her how.
She could not afford to pay the monthly charges for a connection.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 gives two reasons: she 'was afraid of pressing the wrong button and losing money', and she 'did not want to keep asking her busy grandchildren for help'.
steps: Find 'kept it in its box' in paragraph 1
Read the next sentence: fear of losing money; not wanting to trouble her grandchildren
solution.why_others_wrong: A, C and D are not mentioned. The passage gives only the two reasons in option B.
solution.final_answer: Option B: She feared losing money by a wrong press and did not want to trouble her grandchildren.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as something taught in the classes?

options.text: Enlarging the text on the screen

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists making a video call, reading a message and booking a doctor's appointment, and adds enlarging the text and typing by speaking. Opening a bank account is not mentioned.
steps: Also: enlarging the text (C), typing by speaking
Opening a bank account is not listed: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are all stated in paragraph 3, so none of them can be the 'NOT mentioned' answer. Bank accounts appear only in paragraph 2, where pensions are credited to them.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Opening a new bank account

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to Kamala Devi, what helped her most in learning to use her phone?

options.text: The patience of the young volunteer who taught her
The low price of the phone
The printed instruction book that came with the phone

solution.concept: Locating a stated opinion
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says what helped her most 'was not the technology itself but the patience of the young volunteer who taught her'.
steps: Find 'What helped her most' in paragraph 4
solution.why_others_wrong: B and C are never mentioned. D contradicts the passage: at home 'everyone was in a hurry', and she did not want to keep asking her grandchildren.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The patience of the young volunteer who taught her

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author suggest by saying that such a class 'can close other gaps too'?

options.text: The classes also help older people save money on their bills.
The classes bring young and old people closer to each other.
The classes reduce the gap between rich and poor towns.
The classes close the gap between what phones cost and what people earn.

solution.concept: Inference: what a closing remark refers to
solution.explanation: The sentence before it says the young volunteers had rarely spent time with people of their grandparents' age and discover 'stories, advice and humour' they had not expected. The other gap closed is the one between generations.
steps: Context: volunteers learn from the elderly learners
Gap besides the digital one: between generations
solution.why_others_wrong: Money saved (A), rich and poor towns (C) and the cost of phones (D) are not discussed in the last paragraph.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The classes bring young and old people closer to each other.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'bear' as used in the passage ('the loss of independence is harder to bear than the inconvenience')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: bear = endure, put up with
solution.explanation: Something 'hard to bear' is hard to endure or put up with. The passage says losing independence is harder to tolerate than the inconvenience itself.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Carry' and 'hold up' are physical senses of 'bear', and 'produce' is the sense in 'bear fruit'. None fits a feeling that is hard to put up with.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how can traffic noise at night harm a person's health even if it does not fully wake him?

options.text: It disturbs his sleep, and poor sleep over years is linked to high blood pressure and heart disease.
It damages his hearing, and hearing loss over years is linked to heart disease.
It lowers his concentration, and he scores worse on reading tests the next day.
It forces him to take sleeping pills, which over time raise his blood pressure.

solution.concept: Locating a stated chain of cause and effect
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: noise 'disturbs sleep even when the sleeper does not fully wake', and 'poor sleep over months and years has been linked to high blood pressure and heart disease'.
steps: Find 'does not fully wake' in paragraph 2
Noise → disturbed sleep → (over years) blood pressure, heart disease
solution.why_others_wrong: B confuses this with the workers exposed to loud machinery, who lose hearing slowly. C refers to schoolchildren, not night-time sleep; no link between hearing loss and heart disease is made. D (sleeping pills) is never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option A: It disturbs his sleep, and poor sleep over years is linked to high blood pressure and heart disease.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a step some cities have taken against noise?

options.text: Displays at junctions showing the noise level

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists campaigns against honking, displays at junctions and silent zones. Wedding processions appear only in paragraph 3, as an example of why enforcement is unpopular; no city is said to have banned them.
steps: Weddings appear only in para 3, not as a measure
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D are each stated in paragraph 4, so none of them is the 'NOT mentioned' answer.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Banning all wedding processions

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What was the purpose of setting the signals to stay red longer when drivers honked continuously?

options.text: To give pedestrians more time to cross the road safely at busy hours
To measure how loud the junction became at different hours of the day
To identify drivers who honked so that they could be fined later
To make honking prolong the drivers' own wait, so that they would stop

solution.concept: Inference: the logic of an incentive
solution.explanation: Honking was meant to hurry the traffic, but under this experiment it 'only prolonged their own wait'. The design turns honking into something that costs the honker, giving drivers a reason to stop.
steps: Effect of honking under the experiment: a longer red light
So honking defeats its own purpose
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C give purposes the passage never mentions. No fines are linked to this experiment; it works by delay, not by penalty.
solution.final_answer: Option D: To make honking prolong the drivers' own wait, so that they would stop

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why does the author mention a police officer who stops a wedding procession?

options.text: To show that weddings are the main source of noise in Indian cities
To illustrate that enforcing noise rules is socially unpopular as well as difficult
To suggest that the police should stop all processions
To argue that noise rules do not apply to weddings

solution.concept: Inference: the purpose of an example
solution.explanation: The example comes in a list of reasons why 'the difficulty lies in enforcement'. An officer who acts 'can expect little thanks from anyone', showing that enforcement meets public resentment.
steps: Topic sentence: 'The difficulty lies in enforcement'
Example: an officer who acts gets 'little thanks'
solution.why_others_wrong: A overstates: weddings are one source among several. C and D are claims the author never makes.
solution.final_answer: Option B: To illustrate that enforcing noise rules is socially unpopular as well as difficult

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude towards the way city residents treat noise?

solution.concept: Tone: identify the author's judgement
solution.explanation: The author says that accepting noise 'comes at a price', that noise is 'a form of pollution ... not merely a nuisance to be shrugged off', and that we must 'stop regarding noise as normal'. The author disapproves of this acceptance.
steps: Closing: stop regarding noise as normal
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Approving' is the opposite. 'Amused' does not fit a passage about health damage. 'Indifferent' does not fit an author arguing for change.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the phrase 'shrugged off' mean as used in the passage ('not merely a nuisance to be shrugged off')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: shrug off = treat as not worth worrying about
solution.explanation: The author contrasts treating noise as real pollution with treating it as a mere nuisance. To 'shrug off' something is to dismiss it as unimportant.
steps: Contrast: 'pollution with real effects' vs 'a nuisance to be shrugged off'
Shrugging = showing you do not care
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Measured carefully' and 'protested against loudly' are the opposite of shrugging something off. 'Removed quickly' would mean the problem was solved, which is not the sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the term 'non-revenue water' refer to, according to the passage?

options.text: Water supplied free of charge to poor households
Water drawn from rivers and lakes rather than wells
Water that is pumped and treated but never reaches a paying customer
Water that is too dirty to be sold

solution.concept: Locating a definition
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 defines it: 'a large share of the water that is pumped and treated never reaches a paying customer. Engineers call this "non-revenue water"'.
steps: Find the quoted term in paragraph 1
Read the sentence just before it
solution.why_others_wrong: A and D are not mentioned. B confuses the sources of water with what happens to it after treatment.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Water that is pumped and treated but never reaches a paying customer

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of what the passage calls a 'commercial' loss?

options.text: A cracked pipe that leaks underground for months
Water that reaches a home through a broken meter and is never billed
A valve that fails at the treatment plant
Water lost when a storage tank overflows

solution.concept: Applying a definition given in the passage
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 contrasts physical losses (cracks, loose joints, failed valves) with commercial losses: 'water that does reach homes but is never billed, because meters are missing or broken ...'.
steps: Physical loss: water escapes from the network
Commercial loss: water is delivered but not billed
Broken meter, no bill: option B
solution.why_others_wrong: A and C are physical losses named in paragraph 2. D (overflowing tanks) is not mentioned as a loss of either kind.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Water that reaches a home through a broken meter and is never billed

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, can rationing water to a few hours a day make it unsafe to drink?

options.text: People store water in tanks for so long that it becomes stale and unsafe.
The treatment plant has less time to clean the water when supply is rationed.
Private pumps add rust and chemicals to the water as they pull it unevenly.
With little pressure in empty pipes, polluted groundwater can seep in through leaks.

solution.concept: Inference: following a stated mechanism
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'When the pipes are empty, the pressure inside them falls, and dirty water from the surrounding soil can be drawn in through the same cracks through which clean water escapes.'
steps: Rationing → pipes empty for most of the day
Low pressure → dirty water drawn in through cracks: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C give reasons the passage never mentions. Private pumps are said to pull water unevenly, not to add chemicals.
solution.final_answer: Option D: With little pressure in empty pipes, polluted groundwater can seep in through leaks.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why does the author describe the work of reducing water losses as 'less glamorous' than building a new dam?

options.text: It is slow, its results are invisible, and it brings little political credit.
It costs far more than building a new dam and gives poorer results.
It does not save any water, since leaks reappear as soon as they are fixed.
It can be carried out only by foreign engineers with costly equipment.

solution.concept: Inference: understanding a contrast
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the work 'rarely features in election speeches' and that it 'is slow and its results are invisible to the public'. A new dam, by contrast, is visible and wins attention.
steps: Not in election speeches → little political credit
Slow; results invisible to the public
solution.why_others_wrong: B contradicts the passage, which says a saved litre is 'usually far cheaper'. C contradicts 'every litre saved'. D is never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option A: It is slow, its results are invisible, and it brings little political credit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following can be inferred from the last paragraph?

options.text: Cities should stop building treatment plants altogether.
A city should cut the water it loses before rushing to find new sources.
Cities already have more water than they can use.
Water losses cannot be measured accurately.

solution.concept: Inference: the author's conclusion
solution.explanation: The last paragraph says a city 'may not need more of it as urgently as it thinks' and 'may first need to stop losing what it already has'. The priority is to reduce losses before seeking new supply.
steps: Key words: 'may first need to stop losing'
'first' sets a priority, not a ban on new sources
solution.why_others_wrong: A and C go far beyond the cautious 'may' in the paragraph. D contradicts paragraph 4, which describes measuring how much water enters each zone.
solution.final_answer: Option B: A city should cut the water it loses before rushing to find new sources.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: The Water Cities Lose Before It Reaches Homes
How to Install a Storage Tank

solution.concept: A title must cover the main idea of the whole passage
solution.explanation: The passage defines water lost after treatment, explains its causes and consequences, and argues that reducing these losses should come first. Only option A covers this.
steps: Paras 4–5: reduce losses before seeking new water: A
solution.why_others_wrong: B contradicts the author's argument. C and D pick up minor details (tanks, meters) from single paragraphs.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The Water Cities Lose Before It Reaches Homes

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what is the likely effect of making the penalty for business failure 'ruin for life'?

options.text: Entrepreneurs become more careful and fewer firms fail.
Talented people avoid starting firms, and owners keep failing firms going for too long.
Creditors recover more of their money from failed firms.
Courts are able to separate misfortune from fraud more easily.

solution.concept: Inference: the author's argument against the old premise
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the rational response to lifelong ruin 'is not greater care but greater timidity': talented people avoid starting firms, and those who start them 'cling to a sinking venture for too long' while assets lose value.
steps: Author's claim: harsh penalty → timidity, not care
Two effects: fewer start-ups; failing firms kept alive too long: B
solution.why_others_wrong: A is the old assumption the author rejects. C is the opposite: assets lose value while owners cling on. D is about the skill of tribunals, not the effect of harsh penalties.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Talented people avoid starting firms, and owners keep failing firms going for too long.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which two goals, according to the passage, should a well-designed insolvency system try to achieve at once?

options.text: Punishing dishonest borrowers and publishing their names
Lowering interest rates and reducing collateral requirements
Resolving failing firms quickly, and letting honest entrepreneurs make a fresh start
Keeping every failing firm alive and protecting its workforce

solution.concept: Locating a stated pair of goals
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: the system 'must allow a failing firm to be resolved quickly' and 'must allow an honest entrepreneur ... to start again without carrying the old debts'.
steps: Find 'two things at once' in paragraph 3
Goal 1: quick resolution; goal 2: a fresh start
solution.why_others_wrong: A describes the harsh historical approach. B names possible side effects discussed in paragraph 4, not goals. D contradicts the aim of resolving failing firms quickly.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Resolving failing firms quickly, and letting honest entrepreneurs make a fresh start

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, are the two goals 'not always in harmony'?

options.text: Generous discharge always leads borrowers to take loans with no intention of repaying them.
Small firms no longer need loans once business failure is forgiven by the courts.
Quick resolution always destroys the value of a failed firm's assets.
Debt relief that is too generous can cut creditors' recoveries and make credit costlier for small firms.

solution.concept: Inference: identifying a trade-off
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains the tension: creditors who expect to recover little lend less, or at higher rates and against heavy collateral, which 'hurts precisely the small firms the system is meant to encourage'; yet a discharge that is too easy invites abuse. Protecting debtors too generously works against creditors and, through them, against small borrowers.
steps: Fresh start made too generous → creditors recover less
Creditors then lend less, at higher rates, against heavy collateral → small firms hurt
This is the conflict between the goals: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A overstates the passage, which says easy discharge 'invites abuse', not that it always leads to fraud. B is not stated. C contradicts paragraph 3, where quick resolution is meant to preserve value 'before it decays'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Debt relief that is too generous can cut creditors' recoveries and make credit costlier for small firms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'premise' as used in the passage ('Modern insolvency law rests on a different premise')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: premise = a basic idea on which an argument rests
solution.explanation: The previous paragraph described the old 'assumption' that failure was a moral lapse. Modern law 'rests on a different premise': a different underlying assumption, namely that most failure is not dishonest.
steps: Parallel: 'The assumption behind such treatment ...' → 'a different premise'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Building' confuses 'premise' with 'premises' (a building or site). 'Promise' only looks similar. A 'conclusion' is what an argument reaches, not what it rests on.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: Failing Well: Why Insolvency Law Matters for Enterprise
The Prisons Where Debtors Were Once Held
Why Fraud Is Increasing Among Small Firms

solution.concept: A title must cover the main idea of the whole passage
solution.explanation: The passage contrasts the old punishment of failure with modern insolvency law, sets out the two goals of a good system and the balance between them, and ends with failure as 'an expensive lesson rather than a life sentence'.
steps: Para 1: harsh treatment of debtors in the past
Paras 2–4: modern premise, goals and trade-off
Para 5: failure as a lesson, not a sentence: A
solution.why_others_wrong: B covers only the first paragraph. C picks up one detail from paragraph 4. D makes a claim the passage never makes.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Failing Well: Why Insolvency Law Matters for Enterprise

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The example of 'may' and 'shall' is used in the passage to show that

options.text: software cannot translate any legal text
a fluent translation that is slightly inexact can change a party's legal obligations
English legal terms have no equivalents in Indian languages
judges should avoid using the word 'shall'

solution.concept: Inference: the purpose of an example
solution.explanation: The example follows the claim that 'a translation that is fluent but slightly inexact can mislead more dangerously than an awkward literal one'. Replacing 'shall' (an obligation) with 'may' (a permission) changes what a party must do.
steps: Claim: small inexactness can mislead dangerously
solution.why_others_wrong: A overstates: the passage says translation is demanding, not impossible. C is not claimed. D draws a lesson the passage never draws.
solution.final_answer: Option B: a fluent translation that is slightly inexact can change a party's legal obligations

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What do the critics mean when they say that the arrangement 'preserves the very hierarchy it is meant to soften'?

options.text: Translations will be available only to litigants who can afford them.
Lawyers will lose their role in explaining judgments to their clients.
Only the English version stays authoritative, though most citizens cannot read it.
Courts in different states will begin to follow different versions of the law.

solution.concept: Inference: interpreting a critical claim
solution.explanation: The critics' own explanation follows the colon: 'the version that counts is still the one most citizens cannot read'. The ranking of English above Indian languages, which translation was meant to soften, remains.
steps: So English still outranks the translation: C
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D are not mentioned. The hierarchy is between languages, not between rich and poor litigants, lawyers or states.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Only the English version stays authoritative, though most citizens cannot read it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: By saying that 'perfection should not be the enemy of progress', the supporters argue that

options.text: translations should carry the same legal authority as the English original
judgments should in future be written only in Indian languages
software will soon be able to produce perfect legal translations
an imperfect translation is still better than none at all

solution.concept: Inference: the meaning of a maxim in context
solution.explanation: The supporters admit the translation 'may not carry legal authority', but say it still gives the litigant 'the ability to read, in his own words, the reasons for a decision'. An imperfect step is better than none.
steps: The maxim: do not reject an improvement because it is imperfect
Gain claimed: the litigant can read the reasons: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B are changes the supporters do not propose; they accept that the English original remains authoritative. C is a prediction the passage never makes.
solution.final_answer: Option D: an imperfect translation is still better than none at all

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'intelligible' as used in the passage ('law that binds people should be intelligible to them')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: intelligible = able to be understood
solution.explanation: The next sentences speak of a citizen who 'cannot understand' a ruling and say justice 'must also be understood'. 'Intelligible' means understandable.
steps: Context: citizens who cannot understand rulings
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Clever' is the meaning of 'intelligent', a different word. 'Binding' repeats 'law that binds'. 'Lengthy' has no connection with the sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: fixed expression 'be no exception' = be like the others
solution.explanation: The sentence says drowning is a leading cause of child deaths in many countries and that India is like them. 'India is no exception' means India too has this problem.
steps: First half: many countries have this problem
Second half: India is the same
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No expression', 'no excuse' and 'no exclusion' do not form a meaningful phrase that says India is like the other countries.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what bottles and tyre tubes do for a learner
solution.explanation: Empty bottles and tyre tubes are light and full of air. They help a learner stay on the surface of the water, that is, float.
steps: Objects: empty bottles, tyre tubes (full of air)
Purpose: keep the child on the surface
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Sink' is the opposite of what these aids do. 'Shout' and 'sleep' have nothing to do with learning to swim.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the next sentence explains the parents' attitude
solution.explanation: The next sentence says many parents feared that a child who could swim would go into deep water alone. Parents with this fear were unwilling or unsure at first: hesitant.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Delighted' and 'grateful' contradict the fear described next. 'Careless' does not fit parents worried about their children's safety.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the purpose of jumping in after a friend in trouble
solution.explanation: A child might jump in to save a friend who is in trouble in the water. Trainers teach them to throw a rope or bottle instead. The verb is 'rescue'.
steps: Situation: a friend in trouble in the water
Natural purpose of jumping in: to save him
solution.why_others_wrong: Nobody jumps into water to 'scold', 'follow' or 'race' a friend who is in trouble.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'left ______ near water' while adults are away
solution.explanation: The crèche exists so that toddlers are not left without anyone watching them while adults work. 'Unattended' means without supervision.
steps: Purpose of the crèche: someone looks after the children
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Unknown', 'untidy' and 'unhappy' do not describe the danger that supervision removes.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the sentences after the blank show what a label reveals
solution.explanation: The rest of the paragraph explains what a careful reader can learn from the ingredient list and the nutrition table, even that a 'healthy' biscuit is as sugary as a cream biscuit. Read carefully, a label is informative.
steps: Following sentences: what the label tells you
Contrast with the front-of-pack slogans that 'reveal little'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Misleading' contradicts the paragraph, which shows the back label revealing the truth. 'Decorative' and 'expensive' have nothing to do with reading a label carefully.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the purpose of figures per hundred grams
solution.explanation: Because the figures are given for the same quantity (one hundred grams), two products in packs of different sizes can be compared fairly.
steps: Same base quantity for every product
'even when their packs are of different sizes'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Combined', 'consumed' and 'concealed' do not go with 'fairly even when their packs are of different sizes'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'however' and the examples of tricks that follow
solution.explanation: The paragraph lists tricks that keep the rules technically satisfied while hiding the truth: splitting sugar into several names, tiny serving sizes, fruit concentrate in 'no added sugar' drinks. Manufacturers have learned to get around (evade) the rules.
steps: 'however' contrasts with the honest reading of labels
Examples: ways of evading the rules
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Abide by' (obey) contradicts the tricks described. 'Write down' and 'look up' do not describe what manufacturers do with the rules.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'arguing that they unfairly brand foods' shows opposition
solution.explanation: An industry that argues the warnings 'unfairly brand foods as unhealthy' is opposing them. It has resisted them.
steps: Reason given by the industry: the labels are unfair
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Welcomed' contradicts the complaint. 'Printed' and 'invented' do not fit an industry that argues against the labels; the experts, not the industry, favour them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'quietly ______ their recipes to contain less salt and sugar'
solution.explanation: To make recipes 'contain less salt and sugar' is to change their composition: to reformulate them. 'Quietly' fits a change made without announcement.
steps: Object: recipes; result: less salt and sugar
'quietly' = without publicity, which also rules out advertising and publicising
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Advertising' and 'publicising' contradict 'quietly' and do not change what the recipe contains. 'Patenting' a recipe protects it legally but does not reduce its salt or sugar.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (1) may be wrongly used: 'It seems a sensible arrangement: experts with research teams should be able to beat ordinary savers'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'It seems ...' introduces a view the author then questions
solution.explanation: The sentence states the common view: paying experts seems reasonable, because experts 'should be able to beat ordinary savers'. 'Sensible' (reasonable) is correct. The 'Yet' in the next sentence questions this view, which only works if the arrangement first seems sensible.
steps: 'It seems ...' + the expert's advantage = a reasonable-looking arrangement
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Senseless' contradicts the reason after the colon. 'Sensitive' (easily affected) and 'sensational' (causing excitement) are look-alike words with the wrong meaning.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (2) may be wrongly used: 'most actively managed funds fail to outperform the market index ... once their fees are ignored'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: fees make returns worse only when they are taken into account
solution.explanation: Funds fall behind the index 'once their fees are' taken out of their returns. Ignoring the fees would make the funds look better, not worse, so 'ignored' reverses the logic. The correct word is 'deducted'.
steps: Fees reduce what the investor actually earns
Funds fail to beat the index after fees are subtracted
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Overlooked' repeats the error of 'ignored'. 'Waived' means the fees are not charged at all, which would help the funds. 'Ignored' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (3) may be wrongly used: 'After fees ... the average active investor must therefore do better than the market'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: follow the arithmetic of the paragraph
solution.explanation: Before costs, the average active rupee earns roughly the market return. Subtracting fees of a couple of per cent must leave the average active investor behind the market: he does worse, not better.
steps: Before fees: about the market return
After fees: market return minus fees
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Well than' and 'best than' are ungrammatical with 'than'. 'Better' reverses the arithmetic, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (4) may be wrongly used: 'Because it needs no research team and trades rarely, its costs are a fraction of those of an active fund'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'a fraction of' = a small part of
solution.explanation: An index fund needs no research team and trades rarely, so its costs are much lower than an active fund's: 'a fraction of' them. The word is correct.
steps: Cause: no research team, little trading
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A multiple of' and 'double' would make the index fund more expensive, contradicting the cause. 'A fragment of' is used for pieces of objects or texts, not for comparing costs.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (5) may be wrongly used: 'Index funds are not without merits. An investor who owns the whole market owns its weaker companies'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the sentences that follow decide the word
solution.explanation: The paragraph goes on to list weaknesses: owning weak companies, no protection when the market falls, the critics' worry about pricing. 'Not without drawbacks' introduces such a list; 'not without merits' would introduce advantages.
steps: Following sentences: problems with index funds
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Virtues' and 'rewards' repeat the error of 'merits'. 'Merits' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (6) may be wrongly used: 'the humble index fund offers a cheap and opaque way to avoid it'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the closing praise must match the passage
solution.explanation: The passage presents the index fund as straightforward: it 'simply buys all the shares in an index'. Calling the way 'opaque' (hard to understand) contradicts this and sits oddly beside 'cheap' as praise. 'Simple' fits.
steps: The sentence praises the index fund
Paragraph 3: it 'simply buys all the shares'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Obscure' repeats the error of 'opaque'. 'Costly' contradicts 'cheap' and the low costs of paragraph 3. 'Opaque' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
There is many reasons (A) / why customers prefer (B) / the new branch. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: After 'there', the verb agrees with the noun that follows it
solution.explanation: In a 'there is / there are' sentence, the real subject comes after the verb. Here it is 'many reasons', which is plural, so the verb must be 'are': 'There are many reasons why customers prefer the new branch.'
steps: 'There is' → 'There are': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B ('why customers prefer') and part C ('the new branch') are correct. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: There is many reasons

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The new clerk (A) / can able to handle (B) / the cash counter alone. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Can' and 'be able to' express the same ability and are not combined
solution.explanation: 'Can' is a modal verb followed by a base verb; 'able' is an adjective used with 'be'. They cannot be joined. Correct: 'The new clerk can handle ...' or 'The new clerk is able to handle ...'.
steps: 'can' + base verb, or 'is able to' + base verb
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject and part C a correct object and adverb. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: can able to handle

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
In the first week of a new job, (A) / almost every trainee (B) / does a few mistakes. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: In the first week of a new job,

solution.concept: Collocation: we 'make' a mistake, not 'do' a mistake
solution.explanation: The noun 'mistake' collocates with 'make': 'almost every trainee makes a few mistakes'. 'Do a mistake' is not standard English.
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct time phrase. Part B ('almost every trainee') is a correct singular subject. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: does a few mistakes.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
After the complaint, (A) / the regional manager ordered for (B) / an inquiry into the delay. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Order' (command that something be done) takes a direct object, with no 'for'
solution.explanation: To 'order an inquiry' is to command that one be held; the verb takes its object directly: 'the regional manager ordered an inquiry into the delay'. 'Order for' is not standard.
steps: It takes a direct object: 'ordered an inquiry'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct time phrase. Part C ('an inquiry into the delay') uses the correct preposition 'into'. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: the regional manager ordered for

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The sweets that the customer (A) / brought for the staff (B) / tasted deliciously. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Linking (sense) verbs such as taste, smell, look and sound take an adjective, not an adverb
solution.explanation: 'Tasted' here describes the sweets, not the way they performed an action, so it is a linking verb and needs an adjective: 'The sweets ... tasted delicious.'
steps: Verb: 'tasted' = had a certain taste (linking verb)
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject with a relative clause and part B completes it correctly. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Could you please tell me (A) / where is the nearest ATM (B) / of your bank? (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: An embedded (indirect) question uses statement word order
solution.explanation: When a question is placed inside another sentence ('Could you tell me ...'), its subject comes before the verb: 'where the nearest ATM of your bank is'. 'Where is the nearest ATM' keeps the order of a direct question.
steps: Main question: 'Could you please tell me ...?'
'where is the nearest ATM' → 'where the nearest ATM ... is': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct polite request. Part C ('of your bank?') is correct. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: where is the nearest ATM

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
I had my passbook update (A) / at the kiosk near the entrance (B) / before meeting the manager. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: at the kiosk near the entrance

solution.concept: Causative 'have': have + object + past participle
solution.explanation: To say that someone else did the action for you, use 'have something done': 'I had my passbook updated'. The base form 'update' is wrong after the object here.
steps: The passbook was updated (by the kiosk)
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct place phrase. Part C ('before meeting') correctly uses a gerund after a preposition. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: I had my passbook update

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The bank will not release (A) / the gold ornaments until (B) / the borrower does not repay the loan. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: the borrower does not repay the loan.

solution.concept: 'Until' already marks the point at which a negative situation ends; it is not followed by another 'not'
solution.explanation: The meaning is: the ornaments stay with the bank up to the moment the loan is repaid. 'Until' + positive verb expresses this: 'until the borrower repays the loan'. Adding 'not' turns the sentence into nonsense.
steps: Main clause is already negative: 'will not release'
'until' + positive clause marks when that ends
'does not repay' → 'repays': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly uses 'will' in the main clause. Part B is correct. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: the borrower does not repay the loan.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The home loan which I applied for it (A) / last month (B) / has finally been sanctioned. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The home loan which I applied for it

solution.concept: A relative clause does not repeat its antecedent with a pronoun
solution.explanation: 'Which' already stands for 'the home loan' as the object of 'applied for'. Adding 'it' repeats the object: 'The home loan which I applied for last month has finally been sanctioned.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct time phrase. Part C correctly uses the present perfect passive with a singular subject. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The home loan which I applied for it

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The portraits of the bank's founders (A) / were hung in the main hall (B) / on the day of the centenary. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The portraits of the bank's founders
were hung in the main hall
on the day of the centenary.

solution.concept: Hang – hung – hung (objects) vs hang – hanged – hanged (execution)
solution.explanation: Pictures and other objects are 'hung'; 'hanged' is used only for putting a person to death. 'The portraits ... were hung in the main hall' is correct, and the plural subject agrees with 'were'.
steps: Part B: 'were hung': plural verb, correct past participle for objects
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each correct as shown in the steps. 'Hanged' would be wrong here, so B is not an error.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Along the back wall of the strongroom (A) / stands two rows of steel lockers (B) / that are rented to customers. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Along the back wall of the strongroom
stands two rows of steel lockers

solution.concept: With an inverted sentence (place phrase + verb + subject), the verb agrees with the subject that follows it
solution.explanation: The sentence opens with a place phrase, so the subject comes after the verb. The subject is 'two rows of steel lockers' (head noun 'rows', plural), so the verb must be plural: 'Along the back wall ... stand two rows of steel lockers'.
steps: Opening place phrase → subject follows the verb
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct opening phrase; 'strongroom' is not the subject. Part C ('that are rented') correctly agrees with 'lockers'. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: stands two rows of steel lockers

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
It was the cashier, (A) / not the two managers, who was (B) / blamed for the shortfall in the vault. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: not the two managers, who was
blamed for the shortfall in the vault.

solution.concept: In a cleft sentence ('It was X who ...'), the verb after 'who' agrees with X; a 'not ...' phrase in between does not change it
solution.explanation: The sentence highlights 'the cashier': 'It was the cashier who was blamed.' The phrase 'not the two managers' is a parenthetical contrast, so 'who' still refers to 'the cashier', which is singular. 'Who was' is correct.
steps: Cleft structure: It was [the cashier] who ...
'not the two managers' is a contrast set off by commas
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct cleft opening. Part B is correct because 'who' refers to the cashier, not the managers. Part C is a correct passive complement. So none of them has an error.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The branch remains open **between 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.** on weekdays.

solution.concept: Paired prepositions: 'between ... and', 'from ... to'
solution.explanation: 'Between' pairs with 'and': 'between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.'. ('From 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.' would also be correct, but it is not offered.)
steps: Only 'between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.' is correctly paired
solution.why_others_wrong: 'From ... and' and 'between ... till' mix the two pairs. The original 'between ... to' is also mixed, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**My colleague and myself will attend** the training programme in Chennai.

options.text: Myself and my colleague will attend
Me and my colleague will attend
My colleague and I will attend

solution.concept: Subject pronoun 'I' (not 'myself' or 'me') in a compound subject
solution.explanation: The pronoun is part of the subject, so it takes the subject form 'I'. A reflexive pronoun ('myself') is used only when it refers back to a subject already in the sentence. Courtesy also places 'I' last: 'My colleague and I'.
steps: Test: drop 'My colleague and' → 'I will attend', not 'myself will attend'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Myself' cannot act as a subject. 'Me' is an object pronoun. The original uses 'myself' as a subject, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: My colleague and I will attend

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
I **wish you will get** the loan you have applied for.

solution.concept: 'Hope' for something possible in the future; 'wish' for unreal or regretted situations
solution.explanation: Getting the loan is a real possibility, and the speaker wants it to happen. That is expressed with 'hope' + 'will': 'I hope you will get the loan.' 'Wish' + 'will' is not standard.
steps: 'I hope you will get the loan'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Wish you would got' adds a past form after 'would'. 'Wish you get' is not standard. The original 'wish ... will' is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.
solution.final_answer: Option A: hope you will get

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
All staff members **are suppose to** wear their identity cards inside the branch.

solution.concept: 'Be supposed to' (= be expected or required to) always uses the past participle 'supposed'
solution.explanation: The expression is 'be supposed to': 'All staff members are supposed to wear their identity cards.' The '-d' is often missed because it is not heard in speech.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Are supposing to' changes the meaning to 'imagining'. 'Were suppose to' still lacks the '-d' and changes the tense. The original lacks the '-d', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The new mobile app is **very better than** the old one.

solution.concept: Comparatives are strengthened with 'much' or 'far', not 'very'
solution.explanation: 'Very' goes with the positive degree ('very good'); a comparative ('better') is intensified with 'much', 'far' or 'a lot': 'much better than the old one'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'More better' is a double comparative. 'Very good than' cannot take 'than'. The original 'very better' is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The children **enjoyed themselves** at the bank's annual staff picnic.

solution.concept: 'Enjoy' needs an object; when there is no other object, a reflexive pronoun is used
solution.explanation: 'Enjoy' is transitive: we enjoy something, or enjoy ourselves. 'The children enjoyed themselves at the picnic' is correct.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Enjoyed' alone leaves the verb without an object. 'Themself' does not match the plural 'children'. 'Were enjoyed' would mean someone enjoyed the children.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
When the manager slipped on the wet floor, the trainees **could not help to laugh**.

solution.concept: 'Cannot help' (= cannot stop oneself) + gerund
solution.explanation: In the sense 'be unable to stop oneself', 'help' is followed by an -ing form: 'the trainees could not help laughing'. ('Could not help but laugh', with a base verb, is also used, but it is not offered.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Help but laughing' puts an -ing form after 'but', which needs a base verb. 'Could not helped' puts a past form after 'could'. The to-infinitive in the original is wrong, so 'No improvement required' does not apply.
solution.final_answer: Option A: could not help laughing

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
She has been handling the bank's foreign exchange desk **for last five years**.

solution.concept: 'For the last/past + period': the article is required
solution.explanation: A period counted back from now is 'the last five years' or 'the past five years'; the definite article is needed. With a period of time, 'for' is used: 'for the last five years'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Since' needs a point of time, not a period. 'From last five years' is not standard. The original drops 'the', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: for the last five years

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The farmer could not repay even the interest, **let alone of the principal**.

solution.concept: 'Let alone' (= and certainly not) is followed by the same kind of element as the one it is compared with
